tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

Optional comma-separated parent scopes when aggregateBy is a topology scope.
Adds extra label dimensions (e.g. break namespace results down by cluster or zone).

- clusters, networks, zones, hosts, namespaces, owners

- clusters+zones, clusters+hosts, clusters+namespaces, clusters+owners
- zones+hosts, zones+namespaces, zones+owners
- hosts+namespaces, hosts+owners
- namespaces+owners
- networks+zones, networks+hosts, networks+namespaces, networks+owners

Examples:

- aggregateBy=resource, groups=namespaces
- aggregateBy=owner, groups=zones,hosts

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Deployment name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching the stable spec)
  - Security config: same as stable (no additional securityContext set)

- Updated the Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector now matches both versions: app=recommendation-engine
  - Left targetPort as 8080 (as it was). Note: nginx-unprivileged defaults to listening on 8080, so both stable and canary pods are compatible.

Current state
- engine-v2-0: 2/2 ready
- engine-v2-1: 2/2 ready
- Service selects all 4 pods, so traffic will be approximately 50/50 by endpoint count.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine -o wide

Notes and rollback
- Keeping equal replica counts preserves ~50/50 splitting. To bias traffic, change replica counts.
- To instantly revert to stable only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale down/delete engine-v2-1.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the bad PVC.
- Recreated homepage-pvc with StorageClass "standard" (which exists in your cluster).
- Recreated homepage-pod to ensure clean scheduling with the now-Bound claim.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.23
  - Container nginx: Ready, 0 restarts

Notes:
- Since the original PVC never bound, no data was lost. If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), say the word and I can switch it.

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the bad PVC.
- Recreated homepage-pvc with StorageClass "standard" (which exists in your cluster).
- Recreated homepage-pod to ensure clean scheduling with the now-Bound claim.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.23
  - Container nginx: Ready, 0 restarts

Notes:
- Since the original PVC never bound, no data was lost. If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), say the word and I can switch it.

I fixed it.

Root cause:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”.

What I changed:
- Deleted the bad PVC.
- Recreated homepage-pvc with StorageClass "standard" (which exists in your cluster).
- Recreated homepage-pod to ensure clean scheduling with the now-Bound claim.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO, StorageClass: standard)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.23
  - Container nginx: Ready, 0 restarts

Notes:
- Since the original PVC never bound, no data was lost. If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), say the word and I can switch it.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged doesn’t listen on port 80; it listens on 8080. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting http://podIP:80/get_status and /is_ready, causing connection refused and the pod to be marked Unhealthy/NotReady. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed
- Deployment orders/webapp:
  - Updated liveness/readiness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service orders/webapp:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints point to 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Events show the old pod failing probes on port 80, new pod healthy on 8080.

How to verify
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return the nginx welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then browse http://localhost:8080/.

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined. Tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress (or a LoadBalancer/Route if you’re on OpenShift).

deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged doesn’t listen on port 80; it listens on 8080. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting http://podIP:80/get_status and /is_ready, causing connection refused and the pod to be marked Unhealthy/NotReady. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed
- Deployment orders/webapp:
  - Updated liveness/readiness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service orders/webapp:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints point to 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Events show the old pod failing probes on port 80, new pod healthy on 8080.

How to verify
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return the nginx welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then browse http://localhost:8080/.

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined. Tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress (or a LoadBalancer/Route if you’re on OpenShift).

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged doesn’t listen on port 80; it listens on 8080. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting http://podIP:80/get_status and /is_ready, causing connection refused and the pod to be marked Unhealthy/NotReady. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed
- Deployment orders/webapp:
  - Updated liveness/readiness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service orders/webapp:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints point to 10.244.0.25:8080.
- Events show the old pod failing probes on port 80, new pod healthy on 8080.

How to verify
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return the nginx welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then browse http://localhost:8080/.

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined. Tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress (or a LoadBalancer/Route if you’re on OpenShift).

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant any permissions on pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pod read permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch between Service selector and Pod labels:
  - Service nginx (web) had selector app=web.
  - Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it wasn’t routing traffic.

- Wrong targetPort:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root).
  - Service was pointing to targetPort 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service to match the Deployment label and correct port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/Endpoints nginx: 10.244.0.26:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080 for the nginx Service.
- No NetworkPolicies in web blocking traffic; no Ingress configured (not needed for ClusterIP access).

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- curl -sI http://nginx
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx -o wide

Optional improvements
- Make the Deployment more self-documenting by declaring the containerPort:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the nginx container spec.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, create:
  - a NodePort Service, or
  - an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Summary
Root cause was a selector/label mismatch and incorrect targetPort. I updated the Service to select app=nginx and send traffic to targetPort 8080. The Service now has healthy endpoints and should be accessible inside the cluster at http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Mismatch between Service selector and Pod labels:
  - Service nginx (web) had selector app=web.
  - Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it wasn’t routing traffic.

- Wrong targetPort:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root).
  - Service was pointing to targetPort 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service to match the Deployment label and correct port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/Endpoints nginx: 10.244.0.26:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080 for the nginx Service.
- No NetworkPolicies in web blocking traffic; no Ingress configured (not needed for ClusterIP access).

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- curl -sI http://nginx
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx -o wide

Optional improvements
- Make the Deployment more self-documenting by declaring the containerPort:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the nginx container spec.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, create:
  - a NodePort Service, or
  - an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Summary
Root cause was a selector/label mismatch and incorrect targetPort. I updated the Service to select app=nginx and send traffic to targetPort 8080. The Service now has healthy endpoints and should be accessible inside the cluster at http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Mismatch between Service selector and Pod labels:
  - Service nginx (web) had selector app=web.
  - Deployment pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it wasn’t routing traffic.

- Wrong targetPort:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root).
  - Service was pointing to targetPort 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service to match the Deployment label and correct port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - web/Endpoints nginx: 10.244.0.26:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080 for the nginx Service.
- No NetworkPolicies in web blocking traffic; no Ingress configured (not needed for ClusterIP access).

How you can verify
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -- curl -sI http://nginx
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or check endpoints:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx -o wide

Optional improvements
- Make the Deployment more self-documenting by declaring the containerPort:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the nginx container spec.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, create:
  - a NodePort Service, or
  - an Ingress (or OpenShift Route) pointing to Service nginx:80.

Summary
Root cause was a selector/label mismatch and incorrect targetPort. I updated the Service to select app=nginx and send traffic to targetPort 8080. The Service now has healthy endpoints and should be accessible inside the cluster at http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80.

results.taskOutput:
Summary
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) that no node in the cluster matches. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” so the pods stayed Pending and the Service had no backends, causing connection refused.
- Fix applied: I updated the web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on the available node.

What I did
1) Checked your namespace:
- Pods were Pending due to FailedScheduling.
- Deployment: web-app-deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- Service: web-app-service exists and selects app=web-app.

2) Fixed the Deployment:
- Cleared the nodeSelector to allow scheduling on the current node.

3) Verified it’s healthy now:
- Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
- Service endpoints: now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

Why it happened
- Your cluster’s node doesn’t have the label environment=production-gpu. With the nodeSelector in place, the scheduler cannot place the pods anywhere.

Next steps and recommendations
- If you need to constrain placement, either:
  - Label an appropriate node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations/affinity to match real node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic once the app is ready.
- Please retry your frontend call; it should no longer get “connection refused.” If you still see issues, I can run an in-cluster curl test to confirm end-to-end connectivity.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) that no node in the cluster matches. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” so the pods stayed Pending and the Service had no backends, causing connection refused.
- Fix applied: I updated the web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on the available node.

What I did
1) Checked your namespace:
- Pods were Pending due to FailedScheduling.
- Deployment: web-app-deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- Service: web-app-service exists and selects app=web-app.

2) Fixed the Deployment:
- Cleared the nodeSelector to allow scheduling on the current node.

3) Verified it’s healthy now:
- Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
- Service endpoints: now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

Why it happened
- Your cluster’s node doesn’t have the label environment=production-gpu. With the nodeSelector in place, the scheduler cannot place the pods anywhere.

Next steps and recommendations
- If you need to constrain placement, either:
  - Label an appropriate node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations/affinity to match real node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic once the app is ready.
- Please retry your frontend call; it should no longer get “connection refused.” If you still see issues, I can run an in-cluster curl test to confirm end-to-end connectivity.

outputSteps.content:
Summary
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) that no node in the cluster matches. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” so the pods stayed Pending and the Service had no backends, causing connection refused.
- Fix applied: I updated the web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on the available node.

What I did
1) Checked your namespace:
- Pods were Pending due to FailedScheduling.
- Deployment: web-app-deployment had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- Service: web-app-service exists and selects app=web-app.

2) Fixed the Deployment:
- Cleared the nodeSelector to allow scheduling on the current node.

3) Verified it’s healthy now:
- Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
- Service endpoints: now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

Why it happened
- Your cluster’s node doesn’t have the label environment=production-gpu. With the nodeSelector in place, the scheduler cannot place the pods anywhere.

Next steps and recommendations
- If you need to constrain placement, either:
  - Label an appropriate node: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations/affinity to match real node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic once the app is ready.
- Please retry your frontend call; it should no longer get “connection refused.” If you still see issues, I can run an in-cluster curl test to confirm end-to-end connectivity.
